sections.h2: Choices for a fast sale in Charlotte
sections.html:
A Charlotte owner may hire an agent, take a cash bid, or deal directly with an investor who purchases houses in their current shape. Cash trades a slice of price for speed and certainty, while a listing trades time for a bigger audience.

The city is big, and housing varies block to block, so what works for an older bungalow may not suit a newer subdivision house. No matter which you choose, the deed gets recorded at the county, and the 2027 revaluation could change the tax bill a buyer expects.

  • Compare your net, not the headline figure.
  • Ask what repairs, tax proration or closing costs the buyer wants from you.
  • See if the house lies in a local historic district before you plan exterior work.
  • Get your payoff and any lien information early.

Permits, code questions and zoning sit with the city. Assessing and tax collection sit with Mecklenburg County. In practice you will phone three places: the county tax office about your bill, the register of deeds about recording, and the city about permits or a historic district.

Vehicles registered inside the city also carry a $30.00 auto fee, which a buyer moving in from elsewhere will run into at the DMV.

Mecklenburg County reappraises every property to market value as of January 1, 2027. The county revalues every four years, though state law requires it only every eight years at most.

After an initial review of 428,506 residential and commercial parcels, the county reported a median increase of about 15 percent for residential property and about 30 percent for commercial property. New values are scheduled to be announced and notices mailed in early 2027, with appeals open in the months that follow. The city, county and towns set tax rates in the spring and apply them to the new values.

Buyers in 2027 will look at the new assessed value when they estimate their own tax bill, so be ready to explain what the current bill covers.

sections.h2: What to do before the new values arrive
sections.html:
Check what the county has on file for your house today, because the revaluation starts from those details. Staff study recent sales, visit properties and weigh improvements. An extra bathroom that does not exist, a basement that was never finished or a wrong square footage can push the number up in front of a buyer.

  • Open your property record card at Reval.MeckNC.gov and mark any error.
  • Send corrections with photos or measurements if you have them.
  • Tell prospective buyers that new values are due in early 2027.
  • Keep any notice you receive, since owners can appeal after notices go out.

A seller who closes before the new values take effect is not affected by them, but buyers will still ask.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Each bill is due September 1, yet interest does not begin until the first week of the next January. Then the bill is delinquent: 2 percent is added, followed by .75 percent for every further month. State law matches this, with interest starting January 6.

Delinquent owners get notices by mail in February and are advertised in the Charlotte Observer in March or April.

Have the closing office verify that the current bill is paid, and ask the Mecklenburg tax office about any gap bill for a vehicle or other item.

sections.h2: Selling in a Local Historic District
sections.html:
Charlotte designates eight Local Historic Districts, and a commission works with owners to keep each district's character. Planning to alter, renovate or build in one? Learn the commission's process first.

When your house is in a district, tell buyers at the start, since outside changes may need sign-off. Ask city staff which design standards apply to your address. Outside the districts, ordinary building permits still apply to repairs and additions, and unpermitted work is a common reason a sale stalls.

sections.h2: State rules that shape a sale
sections.html:
Several statewide rules affect cost and timing. Under G.S. 105-228.30 the seller pays the deed transfer tax, and recording a deed of trust release at the register of deeds costs nothing under G.S. 161-10.

  • Relief programs: owners may receive only one of three, and the circuit breaker's deferred tax from three prior years comes due on transfer.
  • Foreclosure: the clerk of court hears it, and a sale can be reopened by an upset bid within ten days of at least 5 percent and $750 more.
  • Estates: an affidavit works for a small estate of up to $20,000 in personal property after liens, and the state estate tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2013.

Many Charlotte sellers hold an inherited or tenant-occupied house. If tenants live there when a foreclosure sale happens, those with newer leases may end them on 10 to 90 days' notice.

Lenders and buyers verify that past work had permits. Did you finish a basement, build a deck or replace a furnace without one? Say so early and ask city staff what it takes to fix the gap. A cash buyer may absorb the problem and lower the price. A buyer using a mortgage may insist you fix it first.

Where tenants live in the house, decide early whether the buyer takes over the lease or gets the place empty. Provide the lease, the rent record and any notices you have sent. The length of notice you must give depends on the kind of tenancy, so check with an attorney before you promise a vacant house.

If the house needs serious work, such as a roof, a foundation repair or an aging heating system, get quotes before you choose between a listing and a cash sale. The quotes tell you how much a cash discount really costs you.

sections.h2: What a cash sale means for your timeline
sections.html:
A sale to a cash buyer usually follows a short path. You accept an offer, a title search confirms ownership and liens, a closing attorney prepares the deed and settlement statement, and you sign. The deed is recorded with the register of deeds, your lender is paid off, and you receive the balance.

Ask for proof of funds before you commit to a date. Ask who pays for the title search and which closing costs land on you. In a city this large, an offer that sounds higher can shrink once repairs, tax proration and fees are subtracted, so write each one down.

Before you list or sign, collect the deed, your payoff letter, the latest tax bill and permits for any past work. If you plan to sell in the months around the revaluation, keep the notice you receive, and give buyers a plain explanation of how the new value might change their bill.

faqs.a: Mecklenburg County. Its Office of Tax Administration appraises property and bills the tax, and the county reappraises every four years.

faqs.q: When does the next Charlotte-area revaluation take effect?
faqs.a: The 2027 revaluation uses a January 1, 2027 effective date. New values are scheduled to be announced and notices mailed in early 2027.

faqs.q: How big a change has the county reported so far?
faqs.a: After an initial review, the county reported a median residential increase of about 15 percent and about 30 percent for commercial properties. Those figures can change before final values are posted.

faqs.q: Does the interest-free window match the due date?
faqs.a: No. Bills are due September 1, but no interest accrues until the first week of the following January.

faqs.q: How many historic districts does Charlotte have?
faqs.a: Eight. The city has eight Local Historic Districts and a commission that reviews changes within them.
